claims.text: A predictive, data-driven framework can be applied to control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Optimizing annealing temperature, holding time, and quenching rate can steer the balance of FCC, BCC, and intermetallic phases.
As-cast or conventionally processed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs exhibit multiphase microstructures containing FCC, BCC, and potentially minor intermetallic phases.
The multiphase microstructure arises from complex compositional interactions in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Machine learning can optimize heat-treatment conditions and quenching rates for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Temperature, holding time, and cooling rate are controllable thermal-processing variables relevant to phase evolution.
Nucleation and growth kinetics of constituent phases are mediated by temperature-dependent atomic diffusion.
A data-driven model can integrate processing parameters with observed phase outcomes to predict annealing–quenching profiles.
Tuning the thermal profile adjusts atomic diffusion and phase-nucleation rates.
Adjusting diffusion and nucleation rates can stabilize desired phases while suppressing unwanted transformations.
The optimized protocol will produce a more reproducible and quantitatively predictable phase balance than conventional heat treatment.
The optimized protocol can controllably increase the desired FCC phase fraction relative to competing phases.
A controlled phase-fraction shift can improve mechanical performance.
Traditional empirical heat treatments provide less controllable phase evolution because of sluggish diffusion and competitive phase formation.
Model accuracy depends on the completeness and quality of the training dataset.
Unknown kinetic pathways and complex inter-element interactions may alter the magnitude of phase-fraction changes.
